candidate.derivedAnswer: C: PQ is always equal to the length of an external common tangent.
candidate.answerReason: Equal tangent segments express the two external tangent lengths as 2PT+TT' and TT'+2QT'. Reflection across the line of centers makes those lengths equal, giving PT=QT' and hence PQ equal to either external tangent length.

methods.label: Equal tangent segments and symmetry
methods.explanation:
The useful observation is that two tangent segments drawn from the same point to a circle have equal lengths. This lets us compare the requested segment with the external tangents without knowing either radius.

[Figure 1](figures/1976_AMC_12_Q26_question_fig1.svg)

Let \(T\) and \(T'\) be the points where the internal tangent touches circles \(O\) and \(O'\), respectively. Along this line their order is \(P,T,T',Q\). On the external tangent through \(P\), call the contact points \(U\) and \(V\), respectively; their order is \(U,P,V\). On the external tangent through \(Q\), call the contact points \(W\) and \(Z\), respectively; their order is \(W,Q,Z\). These are the separating and nonseparating tangent arrangements shown: the internal tangent has the circles on opposite sides, and each external tangent has them on the same side.

Equal tangent segments from \(P\) give \(PU=PT\) and \(PV=PT'\). Consequently, the first external tangent length is
\[
UV=PU+PV=PT+PT'=2PT+TT'.
\]
Similarly, equal tangent segments from \(Q\) give
\[
WZ=QW+QZ=QT+QT'=TT'+2QT'.
\]
Reflection across the line joining the centers preserves each circle and exchanges the two external common tangents. Thus \(UV=WZ\), so the two displayed equations imply \(PT=QT'\). Therefore
\[
PQ=PT+TT'+QT'=2PT+TT'=UV.
\]
Here the length of a common tangent means the segment between its two contact points. The argument also applies when the radii are equal. Thus \(PQ\) always equals an external common tangent length, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
